accuracy.evidence: Uses the standard chance vocabulary impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain on a likelihood scale from 0 to 1, the bridge to the KS3 'probability scale from 0 to 1'. Each lab state was checked against the counts: 0 red of 8 is impossible, 4 of 8 is an even chance at one half, 1 to 3 of 8 is unlikely, 5 to 7 of 8 is likely, 8 of 8 is certain, and bags of 2 out of 8 and 2 out of 4 sit at one quarter and one half. All outcomes are equally likely (same-size counters, equal spinner parts).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets counting only the wanted outcomes (two bags with 2 red each but different totals), treating likely as certain (the spinner tally shows blue still turning up), treating unlikely as impossible (step 3 refuses 0 red), and the gambler's fallacy that heads is due after tails (mastery m8). The adult notes name each of these as a common mistake and explain why equally likely outcomes matter.

lab_distinct.evidence: flaglikely combines a draggable pointer on a 0-to-1 scale marked in eighths with a bag of tappable counters and an eight-part spinner whose parts are painted red, plus a 10-spin tally. It passes the 30% shingle gate and differs from flagprob, which writes probability as a fraction of equally likely outcomes, because here the child works with words and positions on the scale.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step fixes one word to one position: impossible is 0 with no red at all, even chance is half the counters, unlikely is between 0 and one half but never 0, likely is more than half yet a 10-spin test still shows blue, and comparing two bags shows the chance depends on the total too. The Challenge applies the words to dice, coins, sweets and spinners.

predictions.evidence: Four of the five build steps ask for a prediction first: the chance of red from an all-blue bag, how many of 8 must be red for an even chance, the word for 1 red in 8, and the word for 6 red parts of 8. Distractors are the true confusions (unlikely for impossible, certain for likely, 8 for half), and the done message quotes the pick back.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six Challenge questions with a tagged reason for each wrong answer in why(): calling an impossible dice roll unlikely or even, favouring heads, calling likely certain, reversing which colour there is more of, comparing bags by the red count alone, and placing even chance at 0. A rule card above the questions lists the five words in order and says likely does not mean always.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday examples (a dice showing 7, heads on a coin, a mostly red spinner) for each word. The adult notes stay in plain sentences and explain why outcomes must be equally likely. Step text is two or three sentences, and the canvas shows the five words under the scale so the child reads the word next to the position.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph does a job: the kid text defines the five words and places them on the line, and the adult text gives the curriculum link, the compare-with-the-total idea, the named mistakes and what each lab step does. The family tip is a pick-and-replace game with socks or bricks. The content gate found no stock phrases, and similarity to other lessons is under 12%.

mobile.evidence: Checked at the iPhone 13 viewport in light and dark: the bag, spinner and scale fit the canvas, the scale words alternate between two rows so they never collide, two bags sit side by side without overlapping, and the paint, pointer and spin buttons are large and wrap. The pointer has a big dashed hit ring, and the browser walk drives every step on desktop and phone.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag or tap has a button twin with an aria-label (move the pointer one eighth towards impossible or certain, make one counter or part red or blue, spin 10 times). say() puts the state into the canvas aria-label and live caption, for example '4 red out of 8 is half: an even chance'. Red and blue counters carry R and B letters so colour is never the only cue, and spinning respects reduced motion.
